imo-isl-2012-a2.title: Residues mod 3, then the sum-set identities
imo-isl-2012-a2.body:
**a) Yes.** Take $A=3\mathbb{Z}$, $B=3\mathbb{Z}+1$, $C=3\mathbb{Z}+2$. Then $A+B\subseteq 3\mathbb{Z}+1$, $B+C\subseteq 3\mathbb{Z}$, $C+A\subseteq 3\mathbb{Z}+2$, which are pairwise disjoint.

**b) No.** Suppose $\mathbb{Q}=A\cup B\cup C$ is such a partition.

*Step 1.* For all $a\in A$, $b\in B$, $c\in C$:
$$a+b-c\in C,\qquad b+c-a\in A,\qquad c+a-b\in B. \tag{1}$$
Indeed, let $u=a+b-c$, so $a+b=u+c$. If $u\in A$ then $a+b\in (A+B)\cap(A+C)$; if $u\in B$ then $a+b\in(A+B)\cap(B+C)$. Both are impossible, so $u\in C$. The other two relations follow in the same way.

*Step 2: $B+C=A+A$ (and symmetrically $C+A=B+B$, $A+B=C+C$).* By (1), $b+c=(b+c-a)+a\in A+A$ for any $a\in A$, so $B+C\subseteq A+A$. Conversely let $a,a'\in A$ and pick $b\in B$, $c\in C$. By (1), $a'+c-b\in B$; applying (1) again to $a$, $a'+c-b\in B$ and $c$ gives $a+(a'+c-b)-c=a+a'-b\in C$. Hence $a+a'=(a+a'-b)+b\in C+B$. So $A+A\subseteq B+C$.

*Step 3.* Without loss of generality $0\in A$. Then $B=0+B\subseteq A+B$ and $C\subseteq A+C$. As $B+C$ is disjoint from $A+B$ and $A+C$, it is disjoint from $B$ and $C$, so $B+C\subseteq A$. Thus $A+A=B+C\subseteq A$; also $A=0+A\subseteq A+A$. Hence
$$A=A+A=B+C .$$

*Step 4.* Now $B+B+B=(C+A)+B=A+(B+C)=A+A=A$ and similarly $C+C+C=(A+B)+C=A$, while $A+A+A=A$. So $3r\in A$ for **every** $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ (take the three summands equal to $r$).

*Contradiction.* Take any $b\in B$ (possible as $B\neq\varnothing$) and $r=b/3\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $b=3r\in A$, contradicting $A\cap B=\varnothing$. ∎

**Answer: a) yes; b) no.**

imo-isl-2012-a4.title: Bounded roots and the rational root theorem
imo-isl-2012-a4.body:
Let $n=\deg f>m=\deg g$.

**Reduction to monic $f$.** Write $f(x)=a_nx^n+\dots+a_0$ and $g(x)=b_mx^m+\dots+b_0$. Put $F(x)=a_n^{\,n-1}f(x/a_n)$ and $G(x)=a_n^{\,n-1}g(x/a_n)$. The coefficient of $x^j$ in $F$ is $a_ja_n^{\,n-1-j}$, so $F$ is monic with integer coefficients; the coefficient of $x^j$ in $G$ is $b_ja_n^{\,n-1-j}$ ($j\le m\le n-1$), an integer. Since $pF(x)+G(x)=a_n^{n-1}\,(pf+g)(x/a_n)$, the polynomial $pF+G$ has a rational root iff $pf+g$ does, and $F$ has a rational root iff $f$ does. So we may assume **$f$ is monic**.

**All roots are bounded.** Because $\deg f>\deg g$, there is $R>0$ with $|g(x)|<|f(x)|$ whenever $|x|>R$. For such $x$ and every prime $p$,
$$|pf(x)+g(x)|\ge p|f(x)|-|g(x)|>(p-1)|f(x)|> 0 .$$
Hence every real root of every $pf+g$ lies in $[-R,R]$.

**Shape of the roots.** The leading coefficient of $pf+g$ is $p$ (as $f$ is monic and $\deg g<n$). If $u/v$ is a rational root in lowest terms with $v>0$, the rational root theorem gives $v\mid p$, so $v=1$ or $v=p$. One of the two cases happens for infinitely many primes.

**Case 1: $v=1$ for infinitely many $p$.** The root $u$ is an integer in $[-R,R]$; there are finitely many such integers, so two distinct primes $p\neq q$ give the same root $u$. Then $pf(u)+g(u)=0=qf(u)+g(u)$, so $(p-q)f(u)=0$ and $f(u)=0$: $f$ has the integer root $u$.

**Case 2: $v=p$ for infinitely many $p$.** Then the root is $u/p$ with $p\nmid u$. Multiply $pf(u/p)+g(u/p)=0$ by $p^{n-1}$:
$$\big(u^n+a_{n-1}pu^{n-1}+\dots+a_0p^n\big)+\big(b_{n-1}u^{n-1}+b_{n-2}pu^{n-2}+\dots+b_0p^{n-1}\big)=0,$$
where $b_j=0$ for $j>m$. Reducing modulo $p$: $u^n+b_{n-1}u^{n-1}\equiv0$, and since $p\nmid u$, $u+b_{n-1}\equiv0\pmod p$. Write $b=b_{n-1}$ and $u=pk-b$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since the root lies in $[-R,R]$,
$$\Big|k-\frac bp\Big|=\frac{|u|}{p}\le R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |k|\le R+|b| .$$
So $k$ takes finitely many values, and some fixed integer $k$ works for infinitely many primes $p$: for all of them $k-\frac bp$ is a root of $pf+g$, i.e. (dividing by $p$)
$$f\Big(k-\frac bp\Big)+\frac1p\,g\Big(k-\frac bp\Big)=0 .$$
Thus the polynomial $h(x)=f(k-bx)+x\,g(k-bx)$ vanishes at infinitely many points $x=1/p$, so $h$ is the zero polynomial. In particular $0=h(0)=f(k)$, so $f$ has the integer root $k$.

In both cases the monic $f$ has an integer root, hence the original $f$ has a rational root. ∎

imo-isl-2012-a4.title: Factor and pigeonhole the factors (sketch)
imo-isl-2012-a4.body: As above, all complex roots of all $pf+g$ lie in a fixed disc $|z|\le R$. If $pf+g$ has a rational root, Gauss's lemma factors it as a product of two integer polynomials of degrees $1$ and $n-1$; since the leading coefficient of $pf+g$ is $p\cdot\mathrm{lc}(f)$, the leading coefficient of one factor, call it $h_p$, divides $\mathrm{lc}(f)$. Passing to infinitely many primes we may assume all $h_p$ have the same degree and the same leading coefficient; their roots are bounded by $R$, so by Vieta all their coefficients are bounded integers. Hence some $h$ equals $h_p=h_q$ for two primes $p\ne q$, and $h$ divides $(pf+g)-(qf+g)=(p-q)f$. As $\deg h\in\{1,n-1\}$, $f$ has a linear factor over $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e. a rational root. ∎

imo-isl-2012-a5.title: Shift by one and show additivity
imo-isl-2012-a5.body:
Put $g(x)=f(x)+1$. The equation becomes
$$g(1+xy)-g(x+y)=\big(g(x)-1\big)\big(g(y)-1\big)\quad\text{for all }x,y, \tag{1}$$
and $C:=g(-1)-1\ne0$. We show $g(x)=x$.

**Values.** $y=-1$ in (1): $g(1-x)-g(x-1)=C\,(g(x)-1)$. $\quad(2)$

$x=1$ in (2): $0=C(g(1)-1)$, so $g(1)=1$. $x=0$: $g(1)-g(-1)=C(g(0)-1)$, i.e. $-C=C(g(0)-1)$, so $g(0)=0$. $x=2$: $g(-1)-g(1)=C(g(2)-1)$, i.e. $C=C(g(2)-1)$, so $g(2)=2$.

**Symmetry about 1:** $g(x)+g(2-x)=2$. $\quad(3)$
Replace $x$ by $1-x$ in (2): $g(x)-g(-x)=C(g(1-x)-1)$. Replace $x$ by $-x$ in this: $g(-x)-g(x)=C(g(1+x)-1)$. Adding, $C\big(g(1-x)+g(1+x)-2\big)=0$, so $g(1-x)+g(1+x)=2$, which is (3).

**Period-like relation:** $g(x+2)-g(x)=2$. $\quad(4)$
Let $u+v=1$. Apply (1) to $(u,v)$ and to $(2-u,2-v)$; note $(2-u)+(2-v)=3$ and $1+(2-u)(2-v)=3+uv$:
$$g(1+uv)-g(1)=(g(u)-1)(g(v)-1),\qquad g(3+uv)-g(3)=(g(2-u)-1)(g(2-v)-1).$$
By (3), $g(2-u)-1=1-g(u)$ and $g(2-v)-1=1-g(v)$, so the right-hand sides are equal. Hence $g(uv+3)-g(uv+1)=g(3)-g(1)$. As $u$ runs over $\mathbb{R}$ with $v=1-u$, $uv=u-u^2$ takes every value $\le\frac14$; so $g(t+2)-g(t)=g(3)-g(1)$ for every $t\le\frac54$. With $t=0$: $2=g(3)-1$, so $g(3)=3$, and (4) holds for $t\le\frac54$. If $x>\frac54$ then $-x<\frac54$, so $g(2-x)-g(-x)=2$; by (3), $g(x)=2-g(2-x)$ and $g(x+2)=2-g(-x)$, so $g(x+2)-g(x)=g(2-x)-g(-x)=2$. Thus (4) holds for all $x$.

**Oddness.** Replacing $x$ by $-x$ in (3): $g(-x)+g(x+2)=2$, and with (4), $g(-x)+g(x)=0$.

**Additivity and multiplicativity.** Apply (1) to $(-x,y)$ and $(x,-y)$, using oddness:
$$g(1-xy)-g(y-x)=(g(x)+1)(1-g(y)),\qquad g(1-xy)-g(x-y)=(1-g(x))(g(y)+1).$$
Adding (and using $g(y-x)+g(x-y)=0$) gives $2g(1-xy)=2-2g(x)g(y)$, i.e. $g(1-xy)=1-g(x)g(y)$. By (3), $g(1+xy)=2-g(1-xy)=1+g(x)g(y)$. Substituting into (1):
$$1+g(x)g(y)-g(x+y)=g(x)g(y)-g(x)-g(y)+1\ \Longrightarrow\ g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y).$$
Then $g(1+xy)=g(1)+g(xy)=1+g(xy)$, so $g(xy)=g(x)g(y)$.

**Conclusion.** $g(x^2)=g(x)^2\ge0$, so $g\ge0$ on $[0,\infty)$; with additivity, $x<y\Rightarrow g(y)-g(x)=g(y-x)\ge0$, so $g$ is nondecreasing. Additivity and $g(1)=1$ give $g(r)=r$ for all rationals $r$. For real $x$ and rationals $r<x<s$ we get $r\le g(x)\le s$; letting $r,s\to x$ gives $g(x)=x$.

So $f(x)=x-1$. Check: $f(1+xy)-f(x+y)=xy-x-y+1=(x-1)(y-1)=f(x)f(y)$, and $f(-1)=-2\ne0$. ∎

**Answer: $f(x)=x-1$.**

imo-isl-2012-a6.title: Chains of the map $n\mapsto n+k_n$
imo-isl-2012-a6.body:
**The orbit of 1.** Let $S=\{1,f(1),f^2(1),\dots\}$. For $n\in S$ there is $k\ge1$ with $f^{2k}(n)=n+k\in S$, so $S$ contains arbitrarily large numbers and is infinite. Hence the numbers $f^i(1)$ ($i\ge0$) are pairwise distinct (if $f^i(1)=f^j(1)$ with $i<j$ the orbit would be eventually periodic and $S$ finite). So each $s\in S$ has a unique *index* $i$ with $s=f^i(1)$, $f$ maps $S$ into $S$, and $f$ is injective on $S$.

**The map $g$.** For $n\in S$ define $g(n)=f^{2k_n}(n)=n+k_n\in S$; it raises the index by $2k_n$ and the value by $k_n$.

*$g$ is injective on $S$.* Suppose $g(a)=g(b)$ with $a<b$ in $S$. From $a+k_a=b+k_b$ we get $k_a>k_b$. Comparing indices, $\operatorname{ind}(a)+2k_a=\operatorname{ind}(b)+2k_b$, so $b=f^{2(k_a-k_b)}(a)$, while also $b=a+(k_a-k_b)$. Thus $k'=k_a-k_b$ satisfies $f^{2k'}(a)=a+k'$ with $0<k'<k_a$, contradicting the minimality of $k_a$.

**Chains.** Let $T=S\setminus g(S)$. Since $g(n)>n\ge1$, $1\in T$. For $t\in T$ let $C_t=\{t,g(t),g^2(t),\dots\}$. Every $n\in S$ lies in some chain: if $n\notin T$ then $n=g(n')$ with $n'<n$ (unique by injectivity), and repeating, the decreasing process stops at an element of $T$. Distinct chains are disjoint: if $g^a(t)=g^b(t')$ with $a\ge b$, injectivity gives $g^{a-b}(t)=t'$, and $t'\notin g(S)$ forces $a=b$, $t=t'$.

Along a chain each step adds $2k$ to the index and $k$ to the value, so if $f^i(1)\in C_t$ and $t=f^{i_t}(1)$, then
$$f^i(1)=t+\frac{i-i_t}{2}. \tag{1}$$

**$T$ is infinite.** Suppose $T=\{t_1<\dots<t_r\}$. By (1), $f^i(1)\le t_r+\frac i2$ for every $i$. Then $1,f(1),\dots,f^N(1)$ are $N+1$ distinct positive integers all at most $t_r+\frac N2$, so $N+1\le t_r+\frac N2$, which fails for large $N$. Contradiction.

**Unboundedness.** Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Take the $k+1$ smallest elements of $T$ and let $t$ be the largest of them. Each of these $k+1$ chains contains a number $\le t$ (its first element). The $k$ numbers $t+1,\dots,t+k$ lie in at most $k$ of these disjoint chains, so some chain $C$ among them contains none of $t+1,\dots,t+k$. Let $n$ be the largest element of $C$ that is $\le t$. Then $g(n)\in C$ and $g(n)>n$, so $g(n)>t$ by maximality and hence $g(n)\ge t+k+1$. Therefore $k_n=g(n)-n\ge t+k+1-t>k$.

Since $k$ was arbitrary, $k_1,k_2,\dots$ is unbounded. ∎

imo-isl-2012-a7.title: Closure under max, min, sums, then positive parts
imo-isl-2012-a7.body:
Write $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$; letters $P,Q$ (with indices) always denote polynomials, and $\mathcal M$ is the set of metapolynomials. Repeating rows or entries does not change a max or a min, so any two metapolynomials can be written with the same $m$ and $n$, and $m,n$ may be enlarged at will.

**Lemma.** For reals $a_{i,j}$ ($i\in[m]$, $j\in[n]$): $\displaystyle\min_{i\in[m]}\max_{j\in[n]}a_{i,j}=\max_{j_1,\dots,j_m\in[n]}\ \min_{i\in[m]}a_{i,j_i}$.

*Proof.* Let $L$ be the left side and choose, for each $i$, $j_i^*$ with $a_{i,j_i^*}=\max_ja_{i,j}$. The choice $(j_i^*)$ gives $\min_ia_{i,j_i^*}=L$, so the right side is $\ge L$. For any choice $(j_i)$ and the index $i_0$ achieving $L=\max_j a_{i_0,j}$, we have $\min_ia_{i,j_i}\le a_{i_0,j_{i_0}}\le L$. $\square$

**Max and min.** If $f_s=\max_i\min_jP^s_{i,j}$ ($s\in[r]$) then $\max_sf_s=\max_{(s,i)}\min_jP^s_{i,j}\in\mathcal M$. For the minimum, $\min_sf_s=\min_s\max_i\big(\min_jP^s_{i,j}\big)$, and by the lemma this equals $\max_{(i_1,\dots,i_r)}\min_s\min_jP^s_{i_s,j}=\max_{(i_s)}\min_{(s,j)}P^s_{i_s,j}\in\mathcal M$.

**Negation.** $-f=\min_i\max_j(-P_{i,j})$, which by the lemma is a max of mins of the polynomials $-P_{i,j}$; so $-f\in\mathcal M$.

**Sums.** $f+g=\max_{i_1}\min_{j_1}P_{i_1,j_1}+\max_{i_2}\min_{j_2}Q_{i_2,j_2}=\max_{i_1,i_2}\min_{j_1,j_2}\big(P_{i_1,j_1}+Q_{i_2,j_2}\big)\in\mathcal M$.

So $\mathcal M$ is closed under sums, differences, max and min, and contains all polynomials.

**Reduction to nonnegative functions.** Let $h^+=\max\{h,0\}$, $h^-=\max\{-h,0\}$; for $h\in\mathcal M$ both are in $\mathcal M$, and $h=h^+-h^-$. Then
$$fg=f^+g^+-f^+g^--f^-g^++f^-g^-,$$
so it suffices to show $fg\in\mathcal M$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal M$ are **nonnegative**.

**Nonnegative case.** Let $f=\max_i\min_jP_{i,j}\ge0$. Since $t\mapsto t^+$ is nondecreasing it commutes with max and min, so $f=f^+=\max_i\min_jP_{i,j}^+$; similarly $g=\max_i\min_jQ_{i,j}^+$. For nonnegative numbers, the product of two maxima is the maximum of the products, and likewise for minima. Hence
$$fg=\max_{i_1,i_2}\ \min_{j_1,j_2}\ P^+_{i_1,j_1}Q^+_{i_2,j_2},$$
and, by closure under max and min, it suffices to show $P^+Q^+\in\mathcal M$ for polynomials $P,Q$. This follows from the identity, valid for all reals $u,v$:
$$u^+v^+=\max\big\{0,\ \min\{uv,u,v\},\ \min\{uv,uv^2,u^2v\},\ \min\{uv,u,u^2v\},\ \min\{uv,uv^2,v\}\big\},$$
applied with $u=P(x)$, $v=Q(x)$ (the right side is a max of mins of polynomials).

*Proof of the identity.* If $u\le0$: the four minima are $\le u$, $\le uv^2$, $\le u$, $\le uv^2$ respectively, all $\le0$, so the right side is $0=u^+v^+$. If $v\le0$ the same holds by symmetry (bounds $v$, $u^2v$, $u^2v$, $v$). If $u,v\ge0$, every minimum contains $uv$, so the right side is $\le uv$; and one of the minima equals $uv$: the first if $u,v\le1$, the second if $u,v\ge1$, the third if $v\le1\le u$, the fourth if $u\le1\le v$. So the right side is $uv=u^+v^+$. $\square$

Hence the product of two metapolynomials is a metapolynomial. ∎

imo-isl-2012-c1.title: A weighted sum that always increases
imo-isl-2012-c1.body:
**The maximum is invariant and all numbers stay positive.** The pair $(x,y)$ with $x>y$ becomes $(c,x)$ where $c=y+1$ or $c=x-1$; in both cases $y\le c\le x$ (indeed $y+1\le x$ and $x-1\ge y$). So no new number exceeds the old maximum $M$, the number $x$ stays, and all entries remain positive integers. Hence at all times every entry is an integer in $[1,M]$.

**Potential.** For the current row $a_1,\dots,a_n$ let $S=a_1+2a_2+\dots+na_n$. If the operation acts on positions $i,i+1$ (with $a_i>a_{i+1}$) and produces $(c,a_i)$, the change of $S$ is
$$d=\big(ic+(i+1)a_i\big)-\big(ia_i+(i+1)a_{i+1}\big)=(a_i-a_{i+1})+i\,(c-a_{i+1}).$$
Here $a_i-a_{i+1}\ge1$ and $c-a_{i+1}\ge0$, so $d\ge1$.

**Conclusion.** $S$ is an integer that increases by at least $1$ at every iteration, but always $S\le M(1+2+\dots+n)$. Therefore only finitely many iterations are possible. ∎

imo-isl-2012-c1.title: Reverse lexicographic order
imo-isl-2012-c1.body:
As above, all entries always lie in $\{1,\dots,M\}$, so only finitely many rows can ever occur.

Compare rows from the right: $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\prec(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ if at the **last** index where they differ, $x_i<y_i$. An operation on positions $i,i+1$ leaves positions $i+2,\dots,n$ unchanged and changes position $i+1$ from $y$ to $x>y$. So each iteration produces a row that is strictly larger in this (total) order. Hence no row repeats, and since there are finitely many possible rows, the process must stop. ∎

imo-isl-2012-c2.title: Bound the total sum, then build the pairs
imo-isl-2012-c2.body:
**Upper bound.** Suppose there are $x$ such pairs. Their $2x$ elements are distinct, so their total is at least $1+2+\dots+2x=x(2x+1)$. The $x$ pair sums are distinct integers $\le n$, so the total is at most $n+(n-1)+\dots+(n-x+1)=nx-\frac{x(x-1)}2$. Hence
$$x(2x+1)\le nx-\frac{x(x-1)}{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ 4x+2\le 2n-x+1\ \Longrightarrow\ x\le\frac{2n-1}{5}.$$
So $x\le\left\lfloor\frac{2n-1}5\right\rfloor$.

**Construction.** Write $n=5k+r$ with $k\ge0$, $r\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}$.

*Case $r\in\{3,4,5\}$*, where $\lfloor\frac{2n-1}5\rfloor=2k+1$. Take the $2k+1$ pairs
$$(3k+2-j,\ 2j)\ \ (j=1,\dots,k),\qquad (4k+2-j,\ 2j+1)\ \ (j=0,\dots,k).$$
The first group has sums $3k+2+j$, i.e. $3k+3,\dots,4k+2$; the second has sums $4k+3+j$, i.e. $4k+3,\dots,5k+3$. All sums are distinct and $\le 5k+3\le n$. The larger elements are $2k+2,\dots,3k+1$ and $3k+2,\dots,4k+2$; the smaller ones are $2,4,\dots,2k$ and $1,3,\dots,2k+1$. So the pairs use each of $1,\dots,4k+2$ exactly once: they are disjoint.

*Case $r=2$*, where $\lfloor\frac{2n-1}5\rfloor=2k$. Drop the pair $(3k+2,2k+1)$ (sum $5k+3$); the remaining $2k$ pairs have distinct sums $\le 5k+2=n$.

*Case $r=1$*, where $\lfloor\frac{2n-1}5\rfloor=2k$. Drop the same pair and subtract $1$ from the larger element of every remaining pair. The larger elements become $2k+1,\dots,4k+1$ except $3k+1$, still all $\ge 2k+1$ and distinct; the smaller elements are $1,\dots,2k$. So the pairs are disjoint, and every sum dropped by $1$: the sums are distinct and $\le 5k+1=n$.

(For $n=1,2$ this gives $0$ pairs, and for $n=3$ the single pair $\{1,2\}$.)

**Answer: $\left\lfloor\frac{2n-1}{5}\right\rfloor$.**

imo-isl-2012-c3.title: Count through the red cell, then AM–GM
imo-isl-2012-c3.body:
We show that in an $n\times n$ table $T\le\frac{4n^4}{27}$, with equality possible when $3\mid n$.

Let row $i$ contain $a_i$ white cells and column $j$ contain $b_j$ white cells, and let $R$ be the set of red cells. A triple is determined by its middle red cell $C_2=(i,j)$, a white $C_1$ in row $i$ and a white $C_3$ in column $j$, so
$$T=\sum_{(i,j)\in R}a_ib_j\le\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in R}\big(a_i^2+b_j^2\big)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(n-a_i)a_i^2+\frac12\sum_{j=1}^n(n-b_j)b_j^2,$$
since row $i$ contains $n-a_i$ red cells and column $j$ contains $n-b_j$ red cells.

For $0\le x\le n$, AM–GM on $2n-2x$, $x$, $x$ gives
$$(n-x)x^2=\tfrac12(2n-2x)\cdot x\cdot x\le\tfrac12\Big(\tfrac{2n}{3}\Big)^3=\frac{4n^3}{27},$$
with equality iff $x=\frac{2n}3$. Therefore $T\le\frac n2\cdot\frac{4n^3}{27}+\frac n2\cdot\frac{4n^3}{27}=\frac{4n^4}{27}$.

**Equality for $n=999$.** Colour cell $(i,j)$ white iff $i-j\equiv1,2,\dots,666\pmod{999}$. Then every row and every column has exactly $666=\frac{2n}3$ white cells, so $a_i=b_j=666$ for all $i,j$, and every inequality above is an equality. Hence
$$T_{\max}=\frac{4\cdot999^4}{27}=148\cdot999^3=147\,556\,443\,852 .$$

**Answer: $\frac{4\cdot 999^4}{27}=147556443852$.**

imo-isl-2012-c4.title: Regular distributions for A, shrinking arcs for B
imo-isl-2012-c4.body:
We prove that for $n\ge7$ boxes the answer is $2n-2$; for $n=2012$ this is $4022$.

### (a) $N=2n-2$: $A$ succeeds

Call a distribution **regular** if $n-2$ boxes hold $2$ coins (*red* boxes) and $2$ boxes hold $1$ coin (*white* boxes). $A$ starts with a regular distribution. We show that after any move $M$ of $B$ she can make the distribution regular again; then every box is always non-empty after her moves.

In every red box $X$, move $M$ moves exactly one of its two coins; call the other one (not involved in $M$) its *spare coin*. Consider the situation

> $(\mathcal S)$: some red box $R$ has two white neighbours and receives no coin from them during $M$.

**If $(\mathcal S)$ does not occur**, let $A$ move the spare coin of every red box in the direction **opposite** to the coin that $B$ moved out of it. This is legal (one coin per box, none involved in $M$). After $M$ and $A$'s move, every red box has sent exactly one of its original coins to each neighbour, and no coin moved twice.

- *Every box is non-empty.* A box with a red neighbour received a coin from it. A box $X$ with two white neighbours must be red (there are only two white boxes) and is unique; since $(\mathcal S)$ fails, $X$ received a coin from a white neighbour during $M$, and $A$ did not move that coin.
- *Every box has at most $2$ coins.* Every box has given away all its original coins (red ones both coins, white ones their single coin in $M$). It receives at most one coin from each neighbour: exactly one from a red neighbour, at most one (its only coin) from a white neighbour.

So all boxes hold $1$ or $2$ coins; since the total is $2n-2$, exactly two hold $1$: the distribution is regular.

**If $(\mathcal S)$ occurs** with box $R$ (neighbours $W_1,W_2$ white), $A$ does the same with all red boxes except $R$, and leaves $R$'s spare coin in place. Then $R$ holds exactly its spare coin. Every other box has a red neighbour different from $R$: each red box $Y\neq R$ is not adjacent to $R$ and cannot have both neighbours white (that would force $n=4$), and $W_1$, $W_2$ have their other neighbour red and $\ne R$ (as $n\ge7$). So every box except $R$ receives a coin from such a neighbour and is non-empty. Each box $Y\ne R$ has given away its original coins, and receives at most one coin from each neighbour (a red neighbour $\neq R$ sends exactly one; $R$ and white boxes send at most their single moved coin). So again all boxes hold $1$ or $2$ coins, and the distribution is regular.

Repeating this forever, $A$ achieves her goal with $N=2n-2$.

### (b) $N\le 2n-3$: $B$ wins

Call a set $\alpha$ of $\ell$ consecutive boxes holding $N(\alpha)$ coins an **arc** if $\ell\le n-2$ and $N(\alpha)\le2\ell-3$.
If an end box of an arc holds $\ge2$ coins, removing it leaves an arc (with $\ell-1$ boxes and at most $2(\ell-1)-3$ coins). So every arc contains an arc whose two end boxes hold at most one coin each.

**An arc exists at the start.** All boxes are non-empty. If some two adjacent boxes $U,V$ together hold at least $N-(2n-7)$ coins, the other $n-2$ consecutive boxes form an arc. For $N\le2n-5$ any pair works (each pair holds $\ge2$). For $N\in\{2n-4,2n-3\}$, the $n$ adjacent pairs hold $2N$ coins in total, so some pair holds at least $\frac{2N}{n}=4-\frac{8}{n}$ resp. $4-\frac6n$, i.e. at least $3$ resp. $4$ coins (as $n\ge7$), which is what is needed.

**Key step.** Suppose all boxes are non-empty and boxes $1,\dots,\ell$ (clockwise) form an arc whose end boxes $1$ and $\ell$ hold exactly one coin (non-empty, at most one). Then $N(\alpha)\ge\ell$, so $\ell\ge3$, and $\ell\le n-2$. Let $B$ pass one coin counterclockwise from boxes $1$ and $n$, and one coin clockwise from every other box. Box $1$ sends its coin out to box $n$, box $\ell$ sends one out to box $\ell+1$, and no coin enters the arc (box $n$ sends to $n-1$, box $\ell+1$ sends to $\ell+2$, and $\ell+1\le n-1$). So the arc now holds $N(\alpha)-2$ coins, and box $\ell$ holds exactly one coin $c$, received from box $\ell-1$ (as $\ell-1\ge2$); $c$ was involved in $B$'s move.

$A$ can bring coins into the arc only into box $1$ (from box $n$) and box $\ell$ (from box $\ell+1$), at most one each. If she brings fewer than $2$, boxes $1,\dots,\ell$ form an arc with fewer than $N(\alpha)$ coins. If she brings $2$, box $\ell$ now holds $c$ (which she cannot move) and the new coin, so it is an end box with $\ge2$ coins; removing it gives an arc with at most $N(\alpha)-2$ coins.

So, as long as all boxes are non-empty after $A$'s moves, $B$ can make the number of coins in a suitable arc strictly decrease (first trimming its ends to single coins). This cannot go on forever, so at some point a box is empty after $A$'s move, and $A$ fails.

**Answer: $N=4022$.**

imo-isl-2012-c5.title: A 3-regular bipartite graph and Hall's theorem
imo-isl-2012-c5.body:
Write A, B, C for the three colours. Let $\sigma$ be the given permutation of squares: the token on square $s$ moves to $\sigma(s)$, with $\operatorname{dist}(s,\sigma(s))\le d$. The rule says: if the token on $s$ is A then the token originally on $\sigma(s)$ is B; if it is B, the token on $\sigma(s)$ is C; if it is C, the token on $\sigma(s)$ is A. Equivalently, for each square $u$:
- the token on $u$ is B $\iff$ the token on $\sigma^{-1}(u)$ is A,
- the token on $u$ is C $\iff$ the token on $\sigma(u)$ is A.

It suffices to move the A-tokens onto the A-squares bijectively with all distances $\le d+2$; the same argument (cyclically relabelling the colours) does it for B and C, and together these give the required permutation.

**Triminos.** Split each row into $n$ horizontal $1\times3$ blocks (*triminos*). The three squares of a trimino have three consecutive values of $x+y$, so each trimino contains exactly one A-square. Two squares of the same trimino are at distance $\le2$.

**The graph.** One side: the $3n^2$ A-squares; other side: the $3n^2$ A-tokens (identified with their original squares $s$). For each A-token on $s$ and each of the three squares $s,\ \sigma(s),\ \sigma^{-1}(s)$, draw an edge from the token to the A-square of the trimino containing that square (multiple edges allowed).

*Edge lengths.* If the chosen square is $w\in\{s,\sigma(s),\sigma^{-1}(s)\}$ and $Q$ is the A-square of $w$'s trimino, then $\operatorname{dist}(s,Q)\le\operatorname{dist}(s,w)+\operatorname{dist}(w,Q)\le d+2$.

*Degrees.* Every A-token has degree exactly $3$. Every A-square $Q$ also has degree $3$: for each of the three squares $u$ of its trimino, exactly one edge arises from $u$ — if the token on $u$ is A, the edge from the token on $u$ (with $w=s=u$); if it is B, the edge from the A-token on $\sigma^{-1}(u)$ (with $w=\sigma(s)=u$); if it is C, the edge from the A-token on $\sigma(u)$ (with $w=\sigma^{-1}(s)=u$). These cases are exclusive and cover all edges at $Q$.

**Hall's condition.** For a set $X$ of A-squares, exactly $3|X|$ edges leave $X$. Their other ends form a set $Y$ of A-tokens which receives at most $3|Y|$ edges, so $3|Y|\ge3|X|$, i.e. $|Y|\ge|X|$. By Hall's marriage theorem there is a perfect matching between A-squares and A-tokens, and all its edges have length $\le d+2$.

Moving each A-token to its matched A-square (and likewise for B and C) gives a permutation in which every token moves a distance at most $d+2$ and lands on a square of its own colour. ∎

imo-isl-2012-c7.title: Caro–Wei bound and averaging over sums
imo-isl-2012-c7.body:
**Lemma.** In a graph $G$ where vertex $v$ has degree $d_v$, there is an independent set of size at least $f(G)=\sum_{v}\frac1{d_v+1}$.

*Proof.* Induction on the number of vertices (the empty graph is trivial). Pick a vertex $v_0$ of minimum degree $d$, with neighbours $v_1,\dots,v_d$. Delete $v_0,\dots,v_d$ and their edges to get $G'$. By induction $G'$ has an independent set $S'$ with $|S'|\ge f(G')$, and $S=S'\cup\{v_0\}$ is independent in $G$. Degrees in $G'$ are at most those in $G$, and $d_{v_i}\ge d$ for $i=0,\dots,d$, so
$$f(G')\ge\sum_{v\in G'}\frac1{d_v+1}=f(G)-\sum_{i=0}^{d}\frac1{d_{v_i}+1}\ge f(G)-\frac{d+1}{d+1}=f(G)-1 .$$
Hence $|S|=|S'|+1\ge f(G)$. $\square$

**Setup.** Let $n=2^{499}$, so there are $2n$ points. Colour each of the chords joining two given points by the sum of its endpoint labels: one of the $4n-3$ values $3,4,\dots,4n-1$. Two chords of the same colour never share an endpoint (the other endpoints would have equal labels). For each colour $c$ let $G_c$ be the graph whose vertices are the chords of colour $c$, two being adjacent when they cross. An independent set in $G_c$ is a set of pairwise disjoint chords with equal sums, so it suffices to find $c$ with $f(G_c)>99$.

**Degrees.** A chord $\ell$ splits the other $2n-2$ points into two arcs; let $m(\ell)\le n-1$ be the smaller number of points. For each $i=0,1,\dots,n-2$ there are exactly $2n$ chords with $m(\ell)=i$ (start at any point and skip $i$ points clockwise; since $i<2n-2-i$ the short side is determined). Such a chord of colour $c$ has degree $\le i$ in $G_c$: every chord of colour $c$ crossing $\ell$ has an endpoint among the $i$ points on the short side, and each of those points is an endpoint of at most one chord of colour $c$.

**Averaging.** Hence
$$\sum_cf(G_c)\ \ge\ \sum_{i=0}^{n-2}\frac{2n}{i+1}=2n\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i,$$
so for some colour $c$
$$f(G_c)\ge\frac{2n}{4n-3}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i>\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i .$$

**Estimate.** Since $n-1\ge2^{400}$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i>\sum_{i=1}^{2^{400}}\frac1i=1+\sum_{k=1}^{400}\ \sum_{i=2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k}\frac1i\ >\ 1+\sum_{k=1}^{400}\frac{2^{k-1}}{2^k}=201 .$$
So $f(G_c)>100.5$, and by the lemma there are more than $100$ pairwise disjoint chords of colour $c$, i.e. with equal endpoint sums. Choosing $100$ of them finishes the proof. ∎

imo-isl-2012-g2.title: Similar triangles $FDG\sim FBE$
imo-isl-2012-g2.body:
**Similar triangles from the circle.** Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, triangles $EAB$ and $EDC$ are similar ($A\leftrightarrow D$, $B\leftrightarrow C$), and so are triangles $FAB$ and $FCD$ ($A\leftrightarrow C$, $B\leftrightarrow D$). Hence
$$\frac{EC}{EB}=\frac{CD}{AB}=\frac{FD}{FB}.$$

**Triangles $FDG$ and $FBE$ are similar.** In the parallelogram $ECGD$ we have $GD=EC$ and $GD\parallel EC$; $CD$ is a diagonal, so $E$ and $G$ lie on opposite sides of $CD$ and $\angle CDG=\angle DCE$ (alternate angles). By inscribed angles, $\angle DCE=\angle DCA=\angle DBA$. Also $\angle FDC=\angle ADC=180^\circ-\angle ABC=\angle FBA$. Therefore
$$\angle FDG=\angle FDC+\angle CDG=\angle FBA+\angle ABD=\angle FBE,$$
and
$$\frac{GD}{EB}=\frac{EC}{EB}=\frac{CD}{AB}=\frac{FD}{FB}.$$
By SAS similarity, $\triangle FDG\sim\triangle FBE$, so $\angle FGD=\angle FEB$.

**Conclusion.** $H$ is the reflection of $E$ in the line $AD=FD$, so $\angle FHD=\angle FED$. As $E$ lies between $B$ and $D$, $\angle FED=180^\circ-\angle FEB$. Hence
$$\angle FHD+\angle FGD=(180^\circ-\angle FEB)+\angle FEB=180^\circ .$$
Finally, $G$ and $H$ are on opposite sides of line $FD$: $E$ lies on segment $AC$ with $A$ on line $FD$, so $E$ is on the same side as $C$; $G=D+(C-E)$ has signed distance to $FD$ equal to that of $C$ minus that of $E$, which has the same sign as for $C$ (as $E$ is strictly between $A$ and $C$); and $H$, the mirror image of $E$, is on the other side. Two opposite angles of quadrilateral $DHFG$ summing to $180^\circ$ means $D,H,F,G$ are concyclic. ∎

imo-isl-2012-g3.title: Equal powers from the incenter
imo-isl-2012-g3.body:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the angles at $A,B,C$ and $I$ the incenter of $ABC$.

**$I_1\in AI$, $I_2\in BI$ and the key equality.** Since $E,F$ lie on the circle with diameter $BC$, $\angle AEF=\beta$ and $\angle AFE=\gamma$: triangle $AEF$ is similar to $ABC$ (with $E\leftrightarrow B$, $F\leftrightarrow C$), with ratio $\frac{AE}{AB}=\cos\alpha$. The similarity is a reflection in the bisector of angle $A$ followed by a homothety at $A$, so it maps the incenter $I$ to $I_1$: $I_1$ lies on segment $AI$ and $AI_1=AI\cos\alpha$. Thus
$$II_1=AI(1-\cos\alpha)=2\,AI\sin^2\tfrac\alpha2,\qquad\text{and likewise}\qquad II_2=2\,BI\sin^2\tfrac\beta2 .$$
The law of sines in triangle $ABI$ gives $AI\sin\frac\alpha2=BI\sin\frac\beta2$. Hence
$$II_1\cdot IA=2\big(AI\sin\tfrac\alpha2\big)^2=2\big(BI\sin\tfrac\beta2\big)^2=II_2\cdot IB .$$
Since $I_1\in IA$ and $I_2\in IB$ (on the same side of $I$ as $A$, $B$), the converse of the power of a point shows that $A,B,I_1,I_2$ are concyclic.

**$CI\perp O_1O_2$.** The line $IA$ meets circle $(ACI_1)$ at $A$ and $I_1$, so the power of $I$ with respect to it is $IA\cdot II_1$; similarly its power with respect to $(BCI_2)$ is $IB\cdot II_2$. These are equal, so $I$ lies on the radical axis of the two circles. So does their common point $C$. Hence $CI$ is the radical axis, and it is perpendicular to the line of centers $O_1O_2$.

**$CI\perp I_1I_2$.** The segment $I_1I_2$ lies inside triangle $ABI$, and the ray from $C$ through $I$ continues beyond $I$ into this triangle, so it meets $I_1I_2$ at a point $Q$ with $I$ between $C$ and $Q$. Then $\angle I_1IQ$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AIC$:
$$\angle I_1IQ=\angle IAC+\angle ICA=\tfrac\alpha2+\tfrac\gamma2 .$$
From the cyclic quadrilateral $ABI_2I_1$, $\angle II_1I_2=\angle ABI_2=\frac\beta2$. In triangle $II_1Q$,
$$\angle II_1Q+\angle I_1IQ=\tfrac\alpha2+\tfrac\beta2+\tfrac\gamma2=90^\circ,$$
so $\angle IQI_1=90^\circ$, i.e. $CI\perp I_1I_2$.

Both $I_1I_2$ and $O_1O_2$ are perpendicular to $CI$, hence parallel. ∎

imo-isl-2012-g4.title: Reflect $Y$ and use powers of $D$
imo-isl-2012-g4.body:
We use directed angles $\angle(\ell,m)$ between lines, modulo $180^\circ$, and signed lengths along a line.

**Setup.** The bisector $AD$ meets the circumcircle again at $P$, the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, which passes through $O$ and the midpoint $M$ of $BC$. Since $AB\ne AC$, the lines $AD$ and $OP$ are different. Let $Y'$ be the reflection of $Y$ in line $OP$. This reflection swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$ and $D\leftrightarrow E$, fixes $P$, and maps the line through $E$ perpendicular to $BC$ onto the line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$. So $Y'$ lies on line $DX$.

**Reduction.** $Y$ and $Y'$ lie on the same side of $BC$ and $\angle BYC=\angle CY'B=\angle BY'C$; so $Y'$ lies on the circle through $B$, $C$, $Y$. Hence it suffices to prove that $B,X,C,Y'$ are concyclic.

**$X,A,Y',P$ are concyclic.** As $OA=OP$, $\angle(AO,AP)=\angle(PA,PO)$. As $YE\parallel PO$ (both perpendicular to $BC$) and $Y$ lies on line $AP$, $\angle(PA,PO)=\angle(YP,YE)$. Reflection in $OP$ reverses directed angles and maps $Y,P,E$ to $Y',P,D$, so $\angle(Y'D,Y'P)=-\angle(YE,YP)=\angle(YP,YE)$. Altogether, using $AX=AO$ and $Y'X=Y'D$ as lines,
$$\angle(AX,AP)=\angle(Y'X,Y'P),$$
which means that $X,A,Y',P$ lie on a circle.

**Powers of $D$.** $D$ lies on chord $AP$ of this circle and on line $XY'$, and on chord $AP$ and chord $BC$ of the circumcircle. Hence, with signed lengths,
$$\overline{DX}\cdot\overline{DY'}=\overline{DA}\cdot\overline{DP}=\overline{DB}\cdot\overline{DC}.$$
By the converse of the power of a point, $B,X,C,Y'$ are concyclic, and therefore $BXCY$ is cyclic. ∎

imo-isl-2012-g6.title: Fixed points on the bisectors and a circle centred at $O$
imo-isl-2012-g6.body:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the angles of $ABC$, and $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$. Note $AE+AF=(b-CE)+(c-BF)=b+c-(c-CD)-(b-BD)=a$; so the three conditions $BD+BF=b$, $CD+CE=c$, $AE+AF=a$ all hold.

**Miquel.** The circles $\omega_A=(AEF)$, $\omega_B=(BFD)$, $\omega_C=(CDE)$ have a common point (Miquel's theorem), which is $P$.

**Lemma.** A circle through the vertex $A$ of an angle of measure $\alpha$ meets the bisector again at $L$ and the sides at $X,Y$. Then $AX+AY=2AL\cos\frac\alpha2$.

*Proof.* As $AL$ bisects $\angle XAY$, $L$ is the midpoint of arc $XY$: $LX=LY=u$; let $XY=v$. Ptolemy in $AXLY$: $AX\cdot u+AY\cdot u=AL\cdot v$. In the isosceles triangle $XLY$, $\angle LXY=\angle LAY=\frac\alpha2$, so $v=2u\cos\frac\alpha2$. $\square$

**Three points independent of $D,E,F$.** Let $\omega_A$ meet line $AI$ again at $A'$ (and define $B'$, $C'$ on $BI$, $CI$ similarly). The lemma for $\omega_A$ gives $2AA'\cos\frac\alpha2=AE+AF=a$. Apply it also to the circle with diameter $AI$ (it meets the sides at the incircle's touch points, with $AX=AY=\frac{b+c-a}2$) and to the circumcircle (which meets $AI$ again at the arc midpoint $M$, and the sides at $B$, $C$):
$$2AA'\cos\tfrac\alpha2=a,\qquad 2AI\cos\tfrac\alpha2=b+c-a,\qquad 2AM\cos\tfrac\alpha2=b+c .$$
So $AA'+AI=AM$, with $A',I,M$ on the ray $AI$. Hence the midpoint of $IA'$ coincides with the midpoint $N$ of the chord $AM$. As $ON\perp AM$, $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $IA'$: $OA'=OI$. Similarly $OB'=OC'=OI$. Thus $I,A',B',C'$ lie on the circle $\Gamma$ with centre $O$ and radius $OI$.

**$P$ lies on $\Gamma$.** If $ABC$ is equilateral, the formulas give $AA'=\frac{a}{\sqrt3}=AO=AI$, so $A'=B'=C'=I=O$; then all three circles pass through $O$, so $P=O$ and $OP=OI=0$. Otherwise $A'=I$ means $a=b+c-a$, and two such equalities would force $a=b=c$; so at most one of $A',B',C'$ equals $I$, say $A',B'\ne I$. Then $A'\neq B'$ (they lie on the different lines $AI$, $BI$), so $I,A',B'$ are three distinct points of $\Gamma$, and it suffices to show that $P$ lies on the circle $IA'B'$; we may assume $P\notin\{I,A',B'\}$. With directed angles modulo $180^\circ$:

*If $P\neq F$:* in $\omega_A$ (through $A,F,P,A'$) and $\omega_B$ (through $B,F,P,B'$),
$$\angle(A'P,FP)=\angle(A'A,FA)=\angle(A'I,AB),\qquad \angle(B'P,FP)=\angle(B'B,FB)=\angle(B'I,AB),$$
so $\angle(A'P,B'P)=\angle(A'I,AB)-\angle(B'I,AB)=\angle(A'I,B'I)$.

*If $P=F$:* then $P\ne D,E$ ($D,E,F$ are distinct, because e.g. $E=F=A$ would give $a=AE+AF=0$), and $P$ lies on all three circles, so
$$\angle(A'P,B'P)=\angle(A'P,EP)+\angle(EP,DP)+\angle(DP,B'P)=\angle(AI,AC)+\angle(CA,CB)+\angle(BC,BI)=\angle(A'I,B'I).$$

In both cases $P,I,A',B'$ are concyclic, so $P\in\Gamma$ and $OP=OI$. (Degenerate coincidences such as $F=A$ are handled by the same angle equalities read with tangent lines, or by continuity.) ∎

imo-isl-2012-g7.title: Compare products along the two sides of the angle
imo-isl-2012-g7.body:
Let $O=BC\cap AD$. The problem is unchanged under relabelling $(A,B,C,D)\to(D,C,B,A)$ (which keeps $E$ and $F$), so we may assume that $O$ lies beyond $B$ and $A$: on line $BC$ the order is $O,B,E,C$ and on line $AD$ it is $O,A,D$. All lengths below are measured from $O$.

**The two circles.** Let $\omega_1,\omega_2$ (centres $O_1,O_2$) be the incircles of $ABED$ and $AECD$. Both are tangent to the lines $OB$ and $OA$, so $O_1,O_2$ lie on the bisector of angle $O$; put $p=OO_1\cdot OO_2$. Since $ABED$ is triangle $ODE$ minus triangle $OAB$, $\omega_1$ is the incircle of $ODE$ and the excircle of $OAB$ opposite $O$. Likewise $\omega_2$ is the incircle of $OCD$ and the excircle of $OAE$ opposite $O$.

If $F$ exists, the incircle of $ABCF$ is tangent to lines $AB$, $OB$, $OA$ on the far side of $AB$ from $O$, so it is the excircle of $OAB$, i.e. $\omega_1$; similarly the incircle of $BCDF$ is the incircle of $OCD$, i.e. $\omega_2$. Let $F_1$ be the point where the tangent from $B$ to $\omega_2$ (other than $BC$) meets $AD$, and $F_2$ the point where the tangent from $C$ to $\omega_1$ (other than $BC$) meets $AD$; both lie on side $AD$. Thus $F$ exists iff $F_1=F_2$ (and then $F=F_1=F_2$ works, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ being tangent to all sides of $ABCF$ and $BCDF$). Here $\omega_2$ is the excircle of $OBF_1$ and $\omega_1$ the incircle of $OCF_2$.

**Lemma.** Circles $\omega,\omega'$ with centres $Z,Z'$ are inscribed in an angle with vertex $O$; $P,S$ lie on one side and $Q,R$ on the other, $\omega$ is the incircle of $OPQ$ and $\omega'$ is the excircle of $ORS$ opposite $O$. With $p=OZ\cdot OZ'$, exactly one of the following holds:
$$OP\cdot OR<p<OQ\cdot OS,\qquad OP\cdot OR>p>OQ\cdot OS,\qquad OP\cdot OR=p=OQ\cdot OS .$$

*Proof.* Let $2\varphi=\angle POQ$, $u=\angle OPZ$, $v=\angle OQZ$, $x=\angle OZ'R$, $y=\angle OZ'S$. Since $PZ,QZ$ bisect the angles at $P,Q$ of triangle $OPQ$, $2u+2v+2\varphi=180^\circ$. In triangle $ORS$ with angles $\rho,\sigma$ at $R,S$, $Z'R$ is the external bisector, so $\angle ORZ'=90^\circ+\frac\rho2$ and $x=90^\circ-\varphi-\frac\rho2$; similarly $y=90^\circ-\varphi-\frac\sigma2$, and as $\rho+\sigma=180^\circ-2\varphi$ we get
$$u+v=x+y=90^\circ-\varphi. \tag{1}$$
Let $h(t)=\frac{\sin(t+\varphi)}{\sin t}=\cos\varphi+\sin\varphi\cot t$, strictly decreasing on $(0^\circ,90^\circ)$. The law of sines in triangles $OPZ$ and $ORZ'$ gives $\frac{OP}{OZ}=h(u)$ and $\frac{OZ'}{OR}=h(x)$; similarly $\frac{OQ}{OZ}=h(v)$ and $\frac{OZ'}{OS}=h(y)$. Hence
$$OP\cdot OR\ \gtreqless\ p\iff h(u)\gtreqless h(x)\iff x\gtreqless u,\qquad p\ \gtreqless\ OQ\cdot OS\iff h(y)\gtreqless h(v)\iff v\gtreqless y .$$
By (1), $x-u=v-y$, so the two comparisons always go the same way. $\square$

**Applying the lemma three times.**
1. $\omega_1$ = incircle of $OED$, $\omega_2$ = excircle of $OBF_1$ ($P=E$, $Q=D$, $R=F_1$, $S=B$): $OE\cdot OF_1$ and $OD\cdot OB$ lie on opposite sides of $p$ (or both equal $p$).
2. $\omega_2$ = incircle of $OCD$, $\omega_1$ = excircle of $OBA$ ($P=C$, $Q=D$, $R=A$, $S=B$): $OC\cdot OA$ and $OD\cdot OB$ lie on opposite sides of $p$ (or both equal).
3. $\omega_1$ = incircle of $OCF_2$, $\omega_2$ = excircle of $OEA$ ($P=C$, $Q=F_2$, $R=A$, $S=E$): $OC\cdot OA$ and $OF_2\cdot OE$ lie on opposite sides of $p$ (or both equal).

If $OE\cdot OF_1>p$, then $OB\cdot OD<p$, so $OA\cdot OC>p$, so $OE\cdot OF_2<p$. Thus $OF_1>OF_2$ and $OA\cdot OC\ne OB\cdot OD$. The case $OE\cdot OF_1<p$ is symmetric. If $OE\cdot OF_1=p$, all four products equal $p$, so $F_1=F_2$ and $OA\cdot OC=OB\cdot OD$.

Hence $F_1=F_2$ iff $OA\cdot OC=OB\cdot OD$, i.e. $\frac{OA}{OB}=\frac{OD}{OC}$, which (with $A,D$ on one ray from $O$ and $B,C$ on the other) means $AB\parallel CD$. So $F$ exists iff $AB\parallel CD$. ∎

imo-isl-2012-g8.title: A common radical centre with the circumcircle
imo-isl-2012-g8.body:
Let $\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C$ be the circles $(AXP)$, $(BYP)$, $(CZP)$, $O$ and $r$ the centre and radius of $\omega$, and $k^2=OP^2-r^2>0$ (as $\ell$ misses $\omega$). Lengths on a line are signed.

**Reduction.** Let $A'$ be the second intersection of $\omega$ and $\omega_A$ ($A'=A$ if they are tangent), so line $AA'$ is their radical axis; define $B',C'$ similarly. Suppose $AA',BB',CC'$ pass through one point $Q$. Then $Q$ has the same power with respect to $\omega,\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C$. Moreover $Q\ne P$, because $P$ has power $0$ with respect to $\omega_A$ but $k^2\ne0$ with respect to $\omega$. So both $P$ and $Q$ have equal powers with respect to $\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C$, and line $PQ$ is the radical axis of each pair. Hence each pair of the circles meets exactly at $P$ and at the second intersection $P'$ of $PQ$ with $\omega_A$: if $P'\ne P$ it is a common point of all three circles, and if $P'=P$ all three circles are tangent to $PQ$ at $P$, hence to each other. (If instead $AA',BB',CC'$ are parallel, the centres of $\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C$ lie on one line through $O$ perpendicular to them, and three circles through $P$ with collinear centres pass through the reflection of $P$ in that line, or are tangent at $P$ if $P$ is on it; the conclusion holds again.)

**Where the radical axes meet $\ell$.** $AA'$ is not parallel to $\ell$: otherwise $OO_A\perp\ell$ ($O_A$ the centre of $\omega_A$), so $O_A$ projects onto $\ell$ at $P$; but $O_A$ projects onto the midpoint of the chord $PX$, giving $X=P$, excluded. Let $X'=AA'\cap\ell$ and similarly $Y'=BB'\cap\ell$, $Z'=CC'\cap\ell$. The power of $X'$ with respect to $\omega_A$ and to $\omega$ is the same:
$$\overline{X'P}\cdot\overline{X'X}=\overline{X'A}\cdot\overline{X'A'}=X'O^2-r^2=X'P^2+OP^2-r^2 .$$
Writing $\overline{X'X}=\overline{X'P}+\overline{PX}$ this becomes $\overline{X'P}\cdot\overline{PX}=k^2$. Put a coordinate on $\ell$ with $P=0$, and let $x,y,z,x',y',z'$ be the coordinates of $X,Y,Z,X',Y',Z'$. Then $-x'x=k^2$, i.e.
$$x'=-\frac{k^2}{x},\qquad y'=-\frac{k^2}{y},\qquad z'=-\frac{k^2}{z}. \tag{1}$$

**Concurrency by Ceva.** Work projectively (parallel lines meet at infinity). Let $U=AA'\cap BC$, $V=BB'\cap CA$, $W=CC'\cap AB$; by Ceva it suffices to show $\frac{\overline{BU}}{\overline{CU}}\cdot\frac{\overline{CV}}{\overline{AV}}\cdot\frac{\overline{AW}}{\overline{BW}}=-1$. Menelaus for the transversal $\ell$ gives $\frac{\overline{BX}}{\overline{CX}}\cdot\frac{\overline{CY}}{\overline{AY}}\cdot\frac{\overline{AZ}}{\overline{BZ}}=1$, so the Ceva product equals the product of the cross-ratios $(B,C;U,X)\cdot(C,A;V,Y)\cdot(A,B;W,Z)$, where $(P_1,P_2;P_3,P_4)=\frac{\overline{P_1P_3}}{\overline{P_2P_3}}\big/\frac{\overline{P_1P_4}}{\overline{P_2P_4}}$.

Projecting line $BC$ from $A$ onto $\ell$ sends $B,C,U,X$ to $Z,Y,X',X$; cross-ratio is preserved, so $(B,C;U,X)=(Z,Y;X',X)$. Similarly $(C,A;V,Y)=(X,Z;Y',Y)$ (project from $B$) and $(A,B;W,Z)=(Y,X;Z',Z)$ (project from $C$). The product of the parts not involving primed points is
$$\frac{\overline{ZX}}{\overline{YX}}\cdot\frac{\overline{XY}}{\overline{ZY}}\cdot\frac{\overline{YZ}}{\overline{XZ}}=-1,$$
so the Ceva product equals
$$-\,\frac{\overline{ZX'}}{\overline{YX'}}\cdot\frac{\overline{XY'}}{\overline{ZY'}}\cdot\frac{\overline{YZ'}}{\overline{XZ'}}=-\frac{x'-z}{x'-y}\cdot\frac{y'-x}{y'-z}\cdot\frac{z'-y}{z'-x}.$$
By (1), $x'-z=-\frac{k^2+xz}{x}$, $x'-y=-\frac{k^2+xy}{x}$, and so on, so the product equals
$$-\frac{k^2+xz}{k^2+xy}\cdot\frac{k^2+xy}{k^2+yz}\cdot\frac{k^2+yz}{k^2+xz}=-1 .$$
Hence $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ are concurrent (possibly at infinity), and by the reduction the three circles have a common point other than $P$ or are mutually tangent at $P$. ∎

imo-isl-2012-n1.title: Multiples of $d$ versus Bézout
imo-isl-2012-n1.body:
**If $\gcd(m,n)=d>1$**, the set $d\mathbb{Z}$ of all multiples of $d$ is admissible (if $d\mid x$ and $d\mid y$ then $d\mid x^2+kxy+y^2$), contains $m$ and $n$, and is not $\mathbb{Z}$. So such pairs fail.

**If $\gcd(m,n)=1$**, let $A$ be any admissible set containing $m$ and $n$. Two consequences of admissibility:

- (i) If $x\in A$ then $cx^2\in A$ for every integer $c$: take $y=x$, which gives $(k+2)x^2\in A$ for all $k$.
- (ii) If $x,y\in A$ then $(x+y)^2\in A$: take $k=2$.

Since $\gcd(m^2,n^2)=1$, there are integers $a,b$ with $am^2+bn^2=1$. By (i), $am^2\in A$ and $bn^2\in A$; by (ii), $(am^2+bn^2)^2=1\in A$; by (i) again, $c\cdot1^2=c\in A$ for every integer $c$. So $A=\mathbb{Z}$.

**Answer: all pairs of nonzero integers with $\gcd(m,n)=1$.** ∎

imo-isl-2012-n2.title: Pin down $x$, then use $503\mid y+z$
imo-isl-2012-n2.body:
Note $2012=2^2\cdot503$ with $503$ prime.

**Finding $x$.** From $x^3(y^3+z^3)-2012xyz=4024$ we get $x\mid4024=2^3\cdot503$. If $503\mid x$, the left side is divisible by $503^3$, so $503^2\mid 4\cdot 503\,(xyz+2)$, i.e. $503\mid xyz+2$; but $xyz+2\equiv2\pmod{503}$. So $x=2^j$ with $j\le3$. If $j\ge2$, then $2^6\mid x^3$ divides the left side, while on the right $xyz+2=2(2^{j-1}yz+1)$ with $2^{j-1}yz+1$ odd, so $v_2\big(2012(xyz+2)\big)=3<6$. Hence $x=1$ or $x=2$, giving
$$y^3+z^3=2012(yz+2)\quad(x=1),\qquad y^3+z^3=503(yz+1)\quad(x=2).$$

**$503\mid y+z$.** In both cases $503\mid y^3+z^3$. If $503\mid y$ then $503\mid z$ as well and we are done; otherwise $503\nmid y,z$. Since $503=3\cdot167+2$, raising $y^3\equiv-z^3$ to the power $167$ gives $y^{501}\equiv-z^{501}$, while Fermat gives $y^{502}\equiv z^{502}\equiv1$. Dividing, $y\equiv-z\pmod{503}$.

So $y+z=503k$ with $k\ge1$. Using $y^3+z^3=(y+z)\big((y-z)^2+yz\big)$ the equations become
$$k(y-z)^2+(k-4)yz=8,\qquad(1)$$
$$k(y-z)^2+(k-1)yz=1.\qquad(2)$$
Note $yz\ge y+z-1\ge502$.

**Equation (1) has no solution.** If $k>4$ then $(k-4)yz\le8$, impossible. Also $y^3+z^3$ is even, so $y+z$ is even and $k$ is even: $k\in\{2,4\}$. For $k=4$: $4(y-z)^2=8$, impossible. For $k=2$: $(y-z)^2-yz=4$, i.e. $(y+z)^2-5yz=4$, so $5yz=1006^2-4$; but $1006^2-4\equiv1-4\equiv2\pmod5$. 

**Equation (2).** Both terms on the left are $\ge0$. If $k\ge2$ then $(k-1)yz\ge502>1$. So $k=1$ and $(y-z)^2=1$; with $y\le z$, $z=y+1$, and $y+z=503$ gives $y=251$, $z=252$.

**Check:** $8(251^3+252^3)=8\cdot31\,816\,259=254\,530\,072$ and $2012(2\cdot251\cdot252+2)=2012\cdot126\,506=254\,530\,072$.

**Answer: $(2,251,252)$.** ∎

imo-isl-2012-n3.title: Primes work; composites have a counterexample
imo-isl-2012-n3.body:
**Primes work.** Let $m=p$ be prime. For $p=2$ the only $n$ is $1$, which divides everything. Let $p$ be odd and $1\le n\le\frac p2$; then $j=p-2n\ge1$. The identity $j\binom nj=n\binom{n-1}{j-1}$ gives
$$(p-2n)\binom{n}{p-2n}=n\binom{n-1}{p-2n-1}.$$
Any common divisor of $p-2n$ and $n$ divides $(p-2n)+2n=p$ and is at most $n<p$, so $\gcd(p-2n,n)=1$. Hence $n\mid\binom n{p-2n}$.

**Composites fail.**
- *$m=2k$ with $k\ge2$:* take $n=k$ (indeed $\frac m3\le k\le\frac m2$). Then $\binom{k}{0}=1$ is not divisible by $k>1$.
- *$m$ odd composite:* write $m=p(2k+1)$ with $p$ an odd prime and $k\ge1$. Take $n=pk$; then $\frac m3\le n\le\frac m2$ (the left inequality is $2k+1\le3k$) and $m-2n=p$. Now
$$\frac1n\binom{n}{p}=\frac{1}{pk}\cdot\frac{pk(pk-1)\cdots(pk-p+1)}{p!}=\frac{(pk-1)(pk-2)\cdots(pk-p+1)}{p!},$$
which is not an integer: $p$ divides the denominator but none of the $p-1$ consecutive factors $pk-1,\dots,pk-p+1$ of the numerator.

**Answer: all primes.** ∎

imo-isl-2012-n4.title: An explicit family; a difference of squares for $a=2$
imo-isl-2012-n4.body:
**a)** Let $k\ge2$, $m=2k-1$, $n=k-1$. Then $m-n=k$,
$$m^2+n=4k^2-3k=k(4k-3),\qquad n^2+m=k^2,$$
so $(m^2+n)(n^2+m)=(4k-3)k^3=(4k-3)(m-n)^3$. Hence every $a=4k-3$ with $k\ge2$ is friendly: $5,9,13,\dots,2009$, which are $502\ge500$ numbers in $\{1,\dots,2012\}$.

**b)** Suppose $(m^2+n)(n^2+m)=2(m-n)^3$ with $m,n\ge1$. The left side is positive, so $m>n$. Write the left side as a difference of squares:
$$(m^2+n)(n^2+m)=\tfrac14\Big[(m^2+n+n^2+m)^2-(m^2+n-n^2-m)^2\Big],$$
and note $m^2+n-n^2-m=(m-n)(m+n-1)$. So the equation becomes
$$(m^2+n+n^2+m)^2=(m-n)^2\Big[(m+n-1)^2+8(m-n)\Big].$$
Thus $(m+n-1)^2+8(m-n)$ is the square of the rational number $\frac{m^2+n+n^2+m}{m-n}$, hence a perfect square. It exceeds $(m+n-1)^2$ and has the same parity as $m+n-1$, so it equals $(m+n-1+2s)^2$ for some integer $s\ge1$. Subtracting,
$$4s(m+n-1+s)=8(m-n),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad s(m+n-1+s)=2(m-n).$$
As $m+n-1+s\ge m+n>m-n$, we need $s<2$, so $s=1$ and $m+n=2(m-n)$, i.e. $m=3n$. But then the left side of the original equation is $(9n^2+n)(n^2+3n)>9n^2\cdot3n=27n^3$, while the right side is $2(2n)^3=16n^3$. Contradiction.

**Answer: b) $a=2$ is not friendly.** ∎

imo-isl-2012-n5.title: Choose $n\equiv -t \pmod p$ with $p-1\mid n$
imo-isl-2012-n5.body:
**These work.** If $a=0$ both radicals are $1$. If $f=ax^m$ with $a\ge1$: for $n=0$ or $1$, $n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}=n$; for $n\ge2$, $\operatorname{rad}(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})=\operatorname{rad}(n)$, so $\operatorname{rad}\big(a\,n^{m\operatorname{rad}(n)}\big)=\operatorname{rad}(a\,n^m)$. In all cases the divisibility holds.

**Nothing else works.** Let $f\ne0$ satisfy the condition; since its coefficients are nonnegative, $f(1)>0$. Write $f(x)=x^mg(x)$ with $g(0)\ne0$. The condition says: for a prime $p$,
$$p\mid f(n)\ \Longrightarrow\ p\mid f\big(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}\big).$$
Since $\operatorname{rad}\big(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)^k}\big)=\operatorname{rad}(n)$, applying this repeatedly gives $p\mid f\big(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)^k}\big)$ for all $k\ge1$.

Let $t\ge1$ with $g(-t)\ne0$, let $p$ be a prime factor of $g(-t)$, and put $n=(p-1)t$. Then $n\equiv-t\pmod p$, so $f(n)\equiv(-t)^mg(-t)\equiv0\pmod p$, and hence $p\mid f\big(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)^k}\big)$ for all $k$.

- If $p\nmid n$: every prime factor of $p-1$ divides $n$, so for large $k$, $p-1\mid\operatorname{rad}(n)^k$, and by Fermat $n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)^k}\equiv1\pmod p$. Thus $p\mid f(1)$.
- If $p\mid n=(p-1)t$: then $p\mid t$ and $g(0)\equiv g(-t)\equiv0\pmod p$.

So every prime factor of every nonzero value $g(-t)$, $t\ge1$, divides the fixed nonzero number $g(0)f(1)$.

**Lemma (Schur).** A nonconstant polynomial $h$ with integer coefficients has infinitely many primes dividing some nonzero value $h(t)$, $t\ge1$.

*Proof.* If $h(0)=0$, then $h(t)$ is divisible by $t$ and the claim is clear (take $t$ prime with $h(t)\ne0$). Otherwise let $c=h(0)\ne0$ and suppose only the primes $p_1,\dots,p_r$ occur; let $Q=p_1\cdots p_r$. Then $h(cQt)=c\,(1+Qt\,r(t))$ for an integer polynomial $r\ne0$. For large $t$, $|1+Qt\,r(t)|>1$ and it is coprime to $Q$, so it has a prime factor outside the list — a contradiction. $\square$

Applying the lemma to $h(t)=g(-t)$ shows $g$ is constant, so $f(x)=ax^m$.

**Answer: $f(x)=ax^m$ with $a,m\ge0$ integers.** ∎

imo-isl-2012-n6.title: Primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$
imo-isl-2012-n6.body:
**Claim.** For every positive integer $y$ there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv3\pmod4$ dividing some $2^ny+1$ ($n\ge1$).

*Proof.* Write $y=2^su$ with $u$ odd, so $2^ny+1=2^{n+s}u+1$; it suffices to find infinitely many primes $p\equiv3\pmod4$ dividing numbers $2^{e}u+1$ with $e>s$. Let $M=2u+1\equiv3\pmod4$, $M=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$. Suppose the set $\mathcal Q$ of primes $q\equiv3\pmod4$ that divide some $2^eu+1$ with $e>s$ is finite, and let $q_1,\dots,q_t$ be those elements of $\mathcal Q$ not dividing $M$. Put
$$L=p_1^{e_1+1}\cdots p_r^{e_r+1}\,q_1\cdots q_t\qquad(\text{odd}),$$
and choose $e=1+j\varphi(L)$ with $j$ large so that $e>s$ and $e\ge2$. Then $2^e\equiv2\pmod L$, so $2^eu+1\equiv M\pmod L$. Consequently $p_i^{e_i}$ exactly divides $2^eu+1$ for each $i$, and no $q_l$ divides it. Every other prime factor of $2^eu+1$ is not in $\mathcal Q$ (it is neither a $p_i$ nor a $q_l$), so it is $\equiv1\pmod 4$. Hence $2^eu+1\equiv p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}=M\equiv3\pmod4$. But $e\ge2$ gives $2^eu+1\equiv1\pmod4$. Contradiction. $\square$

**The problem.** Let $p\equiv3\pmod4$ be a prime dividing $2^ny+1$. Then $p\mid x^{2^n}-1$, so $p\nmid x$ and the order $d$ of $x$ modulo $p$ divides $2^n$; it also divides $p-1$ (Fermat). As $p-1\equiv2\pmod4$, $\gcd(2^n,p-1)=2$, so $d\mid2$ and $p\mid x^2-1$.

By the claim, infinitely many primes divide $x^2-1$. This forces $x^2-1=0$, i.e. $x=1$. ∎

imo-isl-2012-n8.title: Count coincidences and use Cauchy–Schwarz
imo-isl-2012-n8.body:
All congruences are modulo $p$; $P=\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$. For $r\in P$ let $s_r$ be the number of pairs $(a,b)\in P^2$ with $a^2+b^5\equiv r$; so $\sum_r s_r=p^2$. We use that for every $c$ the congruence $x^k\equiv c$ has at most $k$ solutions $x\in P$ (a nonzero polynomial of degree $k$ has at most $k$ roots modulo a prime).

**Counting quadruples.** Let $N$ be the number of $(a,b,c,d)\in P^4$ with $a^2+b^5\equiv c^2+d^5$. Grouping by the common value $r$, $N=\sum_r s_r^2$. On the other hand, fix $(b,d)$:

- If $b^5\equiv d^5$: we need $a^2\equiv c^2$, i.e. $a\equiv\pm c$, which has $2p-1$ solutions $(a,c)$. The number $k$ of such pairs $(b,d)$ is at most $1+5(p-1)=5p-4$ ($b=0$ forces $d=0$; each $b\ne0$ allows at most $5$ values $d$).
- If $b^5\not\equiv d^5$: we need $(a-c)(a+c)\equiv d^5-b^5\not\equiv0$. Choosing $a-c\equiv e\not\equiv0$ ($p-1$ ways) determines $a+c$ and then $a,c$ uniquely (as $p$ is odd). So there are $p-1$ solutions.

Hence
$$N=k(2p-1)+(p^2-k)(p-1)=p^2(p-1)+kp\le p^2(p-1)+(5p-4)p=p(p^2+4p-4).$$

**Many missing residues.** Suppose some $r$ has $s_r=0$; clearly $r\not\equiv0$. Let $T$ be the set of nonzero tenth powers modulo $p$; as each value is a tenth power of at most $10$ residues, $|T|\ge\frac{p-1}{10}\ge10$. For $t=z^{10}\in T$, also $s_{tr}=0$: if $x^2+y^5\equiv tr$, then
$$(z^{-5}x)^2+(z^{-2}y)^5\equiv z^{-10}(x^2+y^5)\equiv r,$$
contradicting $s_r=0$. The residues $tr$ ($t\in T$) are distinct, so at least $4$ residues have $s=0$, and at most $p-4$ values $s_r$ are nonzero.

**Contradiction.** By Cauchy–Schwarz over these at most $p-4$ residues,
$$N=\sum_rs_r^2\ge\frac{\big(\sum_rs_r\big)^2}{p-4}=\frac{p^4}{p-4}.$$
But $\frac{p^4}{p-4}>p(p^2+4p-4)$, since this is equivalent to $p^3>(p-4)(p^2+4p-4)=p^3-20p+16$, i.e. $20p>16$. This contradicts the upper bound for $N$. Hence every $r$ is of the form $a^2+b^5$ modulo $p$. ∎
